column2: Having bowed to Nārāyaṇa, and to Nara, the highest of men,
and to the goddess Sarasvatī as well, one should then recite the Jaya.
Ugraśravas, the son of Lomaharṣaṇa, a bard versed in the ancient lore, at the twelve-year sacrificial session of Śaunaka, the master of the house, in the Naimiṣa Forest,
came up to the brahmin seers of strict vows as they sat at their ease,
bowed low in humility, one day, the son of the bard.
When he had reached the hermitage, the dwellers of the Naimiṣa Forest,
the ascetics, gathered round him there to hear his wondrous tales.
Greeting all those hermits with joined palms,
he asked after the growth of their austerities, and the good ones welcomed him.
Then, when all those ascetics had sat down,
Lomaharṣaṇa's son humbly took the seat that was shown him.
Seeing him seated at his ease and rested,
a certain seer there asked him, to set the tales going:

From where do you come, Sauti, and where have you spent
7.2	this time, lotus-eyed one? Tell me, who ask you this.

At the snake sacrifice of the great-souled royal seer Janamejaya,
8.2	in the presence of that lord of kings, the true son of Parikṣit,
9.1	the many holy tales proclaimed by Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana,
9.2	which Vaiśaṃpāyana duly told there —
10.1	when I had heard them, tales of wondrous meaning that belong to the Mahābhārata,
10.2	and had wandered round many fords and sanctuaries,
11.1	to the holy place called Samantapañcaka, frequented by the twice-born,
11.2	I went, to the land where long ago the war was fought
11.3	between the Pāṇḍavas and the Kurus and all the kings.
12.1	Wishing to see you, I have come from there into your presence here.
12.2	Long-lived ones, all of you I hold to be one with Brahman.
13.1	At this sacrifice, most fortunate ones, radiant as the sun and fire,
13.2	bathed and pure, your prayers muttered, your fires fed,
13.3	you sit at your ease. What shall I tell you, twice-born ones?
14.1	Holy tales founded on the ancient lore, or tales founded on dharma,
14.2	or the deeds of the lords of men and of the great-souled seers?

The ancient lore proclaimed by Dvaipāyana, the supreme seer,
15.2	which the gods and the brahmin seers honoured when they heard it,
16.1	of that best of narratives, wondrous in its words and books,
16.2	endowed with subtle meanings and reasoning, adorned with the meanings of the Veda,
17.1	of the history of the Bhāratas — the holy collection, rich in the book's meanings,
17.2	refined, sacred, amplified by many treatises,
18.1	which Vaiśaṃpāyana told King Janamejaya,
18.2	duly, that seer, gladly, at the session, at Dvaipāyana's command,
19.1	the equal of the four Vedas, the work of Vyāsa of wondrous deeds —
19.2	that collection we wish to hear, righteous, dispelling the fear of evil.

The first Person, the Lord, much invoked, much praised,
20.2	the Truth, the one imperishable syllable, Brahman, manifest and unmanifest, eternal,
21.1	non-being and being, and the universe; beyond being and non-being,
21.2	creator of the high and the low, ancient, supreme, imperishable,
22.1	auspicious, the auspicious one, Viṣṇu, most desired, sinless, pure,
22.2	Hṛṣīkeśa, Hari, guru of all that moves and does not move — having bowed to him,
23.1	the thought of the great seer honoured here in all the world, the great-souled,
23.2	of Vyāsa of boundless splendour, I shall proclaim entire.
24.1	Some poets have told this history, others tell it now,
24.2	and others again will tell it on earth.
25.1	This great knowledge is established in the three worlds,
25.2	and the twice-born keep it, in full and in brief;
26.1	adorned with fine words, with the usages of gods and men,
26.2	set in metres of many kinds, it is dear to the learned.
27.1	When this world was without radiance, without light, covered on every side by darkness,
27.2	there came to be one great egg, the imperishable seed of creatures,
28.1	at the beginning of the age, the great divine cause, as they say,
28.2	in which, it is heard, is the True, the Light, the eternal Brahman,
29.1	wondrous and inconceivable, the same in every part,
29.2	the unmanifest, subtle cause, whose nature is being and non-being.
30.1	From it was born the Grandfather, the sole lord Prajāpati,
30.2	Brahmā, guru of the gods, Sthāṇu, Manu, Ka, and Parameṣṭhin,
31.1	Dakṣa the son of Pracetas, and the seven sons of Dakṣa;
31.2	then came forth the lords of creatures, twenty-one of them,
32.1	and the Person of immeasurable soul, whom all the seers know,
32.2	the All-Gods, the Ādityas, the Vasus, and the two Aśvins,
33.1	Yakṣas, Sādhyas, Piśācas, Guhyakas, and the Fathers;
33.2	then were born the learned, cultivated, stainless brahmin seers,
34.1	and many royal seers, endowed with every virtue;
34.2	the waters, the sky, the earth, the wind, the middle air, and the directions,
35.1	the year, the seasons, the months, the fortnights, days and nights in their order,
35.2	and whatever else there is — all of it came to be, with the world as its witness.
36.1	Whatever is seen here, any creature, moving or unmoving,
36.2	is all drawn in again when the end of the age arrives.
37.1	As in its turn each season shows its signs, of many forms,
37.2	the very same ones, so do beings appear at the beginnings of the ages.
38.1	Thus this wheel, without beginning or end, that brings about the dissolution of creatures,
38.2	never born and never dying, turns round and round in the world.
39.1	Thirty-three thousand, thirty-three hundred,
39.2	and thirty-three: the creation of the gods, told in brief.
40.1	The son of Heaven, Bṛhadbhānu, Cakṣus, Ātman, Vibhāvasu,
40.2	Savitṛ, Ṛcīka, Arka, Bhānu, Āśāvaha, Ravi —
41.1	All are sons of Vivasvat; Mahya was the youngest of them.
41.2	His son was Devabhrāṭ; from him came the one remembered as Subhrāṭ.
42.1	Subhrāṭ had three sons, rich in offspring and deeply learned:
42.2	Daśajyoti, Śatajyoti, and Sahasrajyoti, master of himself.
43.1	Ten thousand sons had the great-souled Daśajyoti;
43.2	ten times as many again were the sons of Śatajyoti here,
44.1	and ten times that again the sons of Sahasrajyoti.
44.2	From them came this line of the Kurus, and the lines of the Yadus and of Bharata,
45.1	the lines of Yayāti and Ikṣvāku, and of the royal seers in every branch;
45.2	many lines came to be, and the creations of beings in their full extent.
46.1	All the dwelling places of beings, and the threefold mystery,
46.2	the Vedas and Yoga, with knowledge, dharma, artha and kāma,
47.1	the treatises on dharma, kāma and artha, and treatises of many kinds,
47.2	and the rules for the conduct of the world — all that had come to be, the seer saw.
48.1	Histories with their commentaries, and scriptures of many kinds:
48.2	here all is gone through in order; this is said to be the mark of the book.
49.1	Having spread this great knowledge out, the seer told it in brief,
49.2	for the learned in the world like to hold it both in brief and at length.
50.1	Some brahmins learn the Bhārata from Manu on, others again from Āstīka on,
50.2	and others from Uparicara on, and they study it well.
51.1	The wise make the varied knowledge of the collection shine;
51.2	some are skilled in explaining the book, others in keeping it in memory.
52.1	By austerity and continence, having divided the eternal Veda,
52.2	the son of Satyavatī made this holy history —
53.1	the son of Parāśara, the learned brahmin seer of strict vows.
53.2	At the bidding of his mother and of the wise son of Gaṅgā, the righteous one,
54.1	in the field of Vicitravīrya, long ago, Kṛṣṇa Dvaipāyana,
54.2	mighty as he was, begot the Kauravas like three fires.
55.1	Having begotten Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Pāṇḍu and Vidura,
55.2	the wise one went back again to his hermitage, to austerities.
56.1	When they had been born, had grown old, and had gone the highest way,
56.2	the great seer told the Bhārata in this world of men.
57.1	Asked by Janamejaya and by brahmins in their thousands,
57.2	he instructed his disciple Vaiśaṃpāyana, who sat near him.
58.1	He, seated with the members of the assembly, recited the Bhārata
58.2	in the pauses of the rites of the sacrifice, urged again and again.
59.1	The breadth of the Kuru line, the virtue of Gāndhārī,
59.2	the wisdom of the Steward, the steadfastness of Kuntī — Dvaipāyana told them truly,
60.1	the greatness of Vāsudeva and the truthfulness of the Pāṇḍavas,
60.2	the misdeeds of the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra — the blessed seer told it all.
61.1	He made the Bhārata collection of twenty-four thousand verses;
61.2	that much, without the side-tales, the wise call the Bhārata.
62.1	Then the seer made a summary again, of a hundred and fifty verses,
62.2	the chapter of contents, of the events together with the books.
63.1	This Dvaipāyana first taught to his son Śuka;
63.2	then the lord gave it to other disciples worthy of it.
64.1	Nārada made the gods hear it, Asita Devala the Fathers,
64.2	and Śuka made the Gandharvas, Yakṣas and Rākṣasas hear it.
65.1	Duryodhana is a great tree made of fury; Karṇa is its trunk, Śakuni its branches,
65.2	Duḥśāsana its abundant flowers and fruit; its root is King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the unwise.
66.1	Yudhiṣṭhira is a great tree made of dharma; Arjuna is its trunk, Bhīmasena its branches,
66.2	the two sons of Mādrī its abundant flowers and fruit; its root is Kṛṣṇa, and Brahman, and the brahmins.
67.1	Pāṇḍu, having conquered many lands by war and by valour,
67.2	then lived in the forest with his people, given to hunting.
68.1	At the killing of a deer in its coupling he met with grievous misfortune;
68.2	from the birth of the Pārthas on, there is the order of their rites of conduct,
69.1	and how the two mothers, by a secret law of dharma, went to
69.2	Dharma, Vāyu, Śakra, and the two gods the Aśvins.
70.1	They grew up with the ascetics, guarded by their two mothers,
70.2	in pure and holy forests and in the hermitages of great men.
71.1	Then the seers themselves brought them to the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra,
71.2	handsome children with matted hair, students of the Veda:
72.1	These are your sons and brothers, your disciples and friends;
these are the Pāṇḍavas." So saying, the hermits vanished.
Seeing the Pāṇḍavas presented by them, the Kauravas
and the cultured classes and the townsmen cried out loudly for joy.
Some said, "They are not his"; others, "They are his";
others, "Since Pāṇḍu is long dead, how are they his?"

Welcome in every way! By good fortune we see Pāṇḍu's offspring.
75.2	Let welcome be spoken! — such words were heard on every side.
When that clamour died away, making all the directions resound,
a tumultuous noise arose from beings who could not be seen.
A rain of flowers, sweet scents, the sound of conches and drums
were there at the Pārthas' entry; it was like a marvel.
And from the delight of all the townsmen at this, born of joy,
a great sound rose there, touching heaven, increasing their fame.
They too, having studied all the Vedas and treatises of many kinds,
the Pāṇḍavas, lived there, honoured, fearing nothing from anywhere.
The subjects were pleased by Yudhiṣṭhira's purity,
by Bhīmasena's steadfastness and Arjuna's valour,
by Kuntī's service to her elders and the modesty of the twins;
the whole world was content with their heroism and their virtue.
Then, in a gathering of kings, the maiden who chose her husband herself,
Kṛṣṇā, Arjuna won, having done a deed most hard to do.
From then on he was honoured in this world by all who bear the bow,
and in battles he became hard to look at, like the sun.
He, having conquered all the kings and all the great hosts,
Arjuna brought the king the Rājasūya, the great rite.
Rich in food, rich in fees, endowed with every virtue,
the great rite Rājasūya was achieved by Yudhiṣṭhira,
through the good counsel of Vāsudeva and the strength of Bhīma and Arjuna,
having had Jarāsaṃdha killed, and the Caidya, proud of his strength.
To Duryodhana came the gifts of homage from every side:
gems, gold, jewels, cattle, elephants, horses and riches.
Seeing that prosperity of the Pāṇḍavas so abundant,
a very great anger, born of envy, arose in him.
And the hall like a flying palace, well built by Maya,
presented to the Pāṇḍavas — seeing it, he burned with grief,
the hall where he was laughed at, as if stumbling in confusion,
in front of Vāsudeva, by Bhīma, as though he were low-born.
Though he enjoyed pleasures of many kinds and jewels of many kinds,
he was reported to Dhṛtarāṣṭra as pale, sallow and thin.
Then Dhṛtarāṣṭra, fond of his son, allowed the dicing;
hearing of it, a great anger arose in Vāsudeva.
He was not much pleased in his mind, yet he approved the quarrels,
and he overlooked the terrible wrongs, the dicing and the rest, as they grew.
Setting aside Vidura, Droṇa, Bhīṣma and Kṛpa, son of Śaradvat,
in that tumultuous war the warriors slew one another.
When the sons of Pāṇḍu were winning, hearing news most unwelcome,
knowing the mind of Duryodhana, of Karṇa and of Śakuni,
Dhṛtarāṣṭra, after pondering long, spoke these words to Saṃjaya:
